claims.text: Local chemical short-range order is the primary mediator of enhanced strength in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Chemical short-range-order regions act as dislocation-pinning centers during deformation.
Short-range-order-mediated dislocation pinning controls the onset of failure.
Homogenized multi-component concentrated alloys can have minimal inherent short-range order.
Controlled annealing promotes chemical short-range order.
Rapid quenching suppresses chemical short-range order.
Annealing and rapid quenching can generate different short-range-order distributions at constant overall composition.
Increased short-range order enhances interactions between dislocations and local lattice distortions.
Enhanced dislocation–lattice-distortion interactions produce more frequent dislocation-pinning events.
More frequent dislocation pinning increases yield strength.
More frequent dislocation pinning modifies deformation behavior.
Annealed samples with promoted short-range order will have higher yield strength than quenched samples.
Annealed samples with promoted short-range order will exhibit more frequent dislocation-pinning events than quenched samples.
Annealed samples with promoted short-range order will exhibit more intermittent dislocation motion than quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched baseline samples will contain less short-range order.
Rapidly quenched baseline samples will have lower yield strength and fewer pinning events.
The effect of short-range order on dislocation dynamics is strongest when chemical complexity and lattice distortion are significant.
The proposed effect should persist across a range of deformation rates and from near-room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures.
Quantifying short-range order and directly correlating it with dislocation-pinning events is experimentally challenging.
A lack of statistically significant increases in both pinning events and yield strength in annealed samples relative to quenched controls would falsify the hypothesis.
